title: skill.spec.jsonc
description: Everything about a skill that the agent must NOT read. Sits beside SKILL.md. The eval reads this file; the agent never does. There is deliberately no `personas` key: the primitive is the domain, and a persona is a maintained selection over domain plus posture (spec/personas.yaml). A per-skill persona list would make every persona rename a 142-file edit.

$schema.description: Points at this schema so editors validate on save. Permitted explicitly because additionalProperties is false and every shipped sidecar carries one.

id.description: Equals the SKILL.md name and the containing directory name.

domain.description: One slug from spec/taxonomy.yaml. Also the parent directory under skills/. Stripped on install.

value.description: Why this skill is worth shipping. It must claim at least one of the first four. Claiming only `convenience-only` is a reject, meaning the model already does this correctly and a skill would add a description to the selection surface and nothing else. That rejection is enforced by the linter rather than by this schema, so it can explain itself instead of only failing validation.

correction.description: The wrong belief this skill overwrites, in at least one complete sentence. If you cannot state it, the skill is not ready. This is the rule most likely to be argued with, which is why it is checked rather than reviewed.

value_probe.description: The measurement that decides whether this skill earns its place: one task, asked twice, once with the skill and once without. Optional here so the forty skills written before it still validate; the value gate requires it of any skill it is asked to measure. Everything in it is written by the author, and the two lists become the grading key, so it is written BEFORE any answer is read. A key written afterwards grades the answers it already saw.

task.description: A concrete job a user would actually bring, in their words, several sentences long. It MUST NOT name the technique, the feature, the error number or this skill, because a question that names the answer is answered by the naming and measures nothing. Describe the symptom or the goal, show the code if there is code, and ask for something specific back. The implicit triggering scenarios are the seed; this is one of them opened out into a task.

states.description: The presence limb. Each entry is one property a correct answer asserts, judged present or absent, nothing in between. Assert a PROPERTY, never a PATTERN: a limb that encodes one route to correctness will mark a differently-correct answer wrong, which happened once here and cost the run its meaning.

refutes.description: The falsehood limb, and the reason this block exists. Each entry is one specific false claim, judged asserted or not asserted. Answer the question: what would somebody confidently say about this that is wrong? A skill's real contribution is often stopping an answer containing something false rather than adding a fact, and a rubric that scores only presence cannot see that. Measured here: a no-skill answer scored a clean six of six while asserting MERGE has atomicity gaps under concurrent writers, which this repository's own runs disprove at eight of eight sessions. Neither skill-loaded arm said it, and presence alone called that a tie.

gate.description: The approach this skill exists to teach, written as one thing an answer either reaches or does not. It is graded on both arms, and it is not a limb, it is the condition the limbs are counted under. The with-skill arm must clear it or `states` and `refutes` do not count at all, because an answer earns no credit for stating a correct fact on the way past the wrong solution: a recovery answer that quotes the retention window accurately and then writes RESTORE DATABASE has helped nobody, and a rubric that adds up its true sentences will score it well. The without-skill arm clearing it is a signal in its own right, and the one this block is least comfortable reporting, because it says the model already gets there unaided and the skill is buying less than its author believes. This mirrors a gating check published by the Supabase team.

posture.description: Descriptive only. NEVER an authorization control: a persona changes what is installed, never what is permitted.

maturity.description: How much has actually been RUN against this skill, decided from evidence in this repository rather than from how finished it feels. Written down on 2026-09-04 because it had never been defined: an audit found 34 sidecars saying draft and 6 saying preview with no criterion anywhere, so the field recorded a mood. Every skill in skills/ lints clean or `npm test` fails, so a clean lint is the floor for all three values and separates none of them. `draft`: nothing has run against it that could have contradicted it. In practice it carries no entries in validation.probes, or the probes it carries did not run and pass in the most recent eval/reports/live/live-eval.json, including the case where validation.target is `cloud` and the run therefore deferred it. scripts/promote.mjs refuses to promote this value, with no override flag. `preview`: validation.probes is non-empty and every one of those probes ran and passed in the most recent live lane run, so the skill's own claims about the engine have been put in front of an engine and held. What is still unknown is whether the skill changes an ANSWER. `ga`: preview, plus the value gate satisfied for this skill, meaning eval/reports/value/<id>.json exists, is current, and either carries a decisive verdict or is accompanied by an accepted <id>.decision.md. Exactly one skill in the corpus can reach this today. Two things this deliberately does NOT use. Routing is not a criterion: docs/how-it-works.md section 8 records that no number in eval/reports/triggering-eval.json has ever been measured twice at a fixed catalog hash, so a threshold on `routed` or on the false positive counts is a coin toss with a policy attached, and the routing gate checks that the evidence is current and gates none of the numbers. A cloud-only skill cannot be decided at all: no cloud lane exists yet, so its maturity records what can be checked and says nothing about the skill. The rule that makes all three usable: evidence sets the CEILING and an author may always declare a value BELOW it. dev-container-templates lints clean with eight green probes and is draft on purpose, because the templates it describes wait on other work and nothing mechanical can see that. Nobody may declare a value ABOVE the ceiling.

applies_to.description: Scope is fixed and the linter enforces it. Managed Instance, Fabric SQL and SQL Server on VMs are not values here and never will be.

related.description: Must resolve to other catalog ids, checked in CI. On fan-out, any entry outside the copied subset is rewritten to a canonical catalog URL or dropped.

target.description: Which substrate lane 4 runs this against, and with it which instrument decides `maturity`. `container` and `both` have an engine, so `preview` requires at least one probe that opened a database connection: a `sql` probe, or a `cmd` probe carrying `engine: true`. `cloud` has no lane yet, so its probes are always deferred. `none` DECLARES THAT THE SKILL HAS NO ENGINE SURFACE, which is the one route past the engine requirement, and it is checked rather than believed: scripts/check-maturity-drift.mjs reads the skill's own SKILL.md and FAILS the declaration if the body names an engine message number, reads SERVERPROPERTY, carries T-SQL or runs a query with sqlcmd. A skill that tells a reader what the engine does has an engine surface whatever this field says. Such a skill is then judged by whatever instrument does fit it, which for azuresql-db-feedback is an HTTPS redirect, and it can reach `preview` on that.

probes.description: The executable half of this block, and what `assert` becomes as the corpus is migrated. Each entry is one claim about what the ENGINE does, written so a runner can settle it: a complete statement, and the outcome that statement must produce. `assert` holds sentences a person reads and nothing executes, which is how 288 hand-written assertions across the catalog came to be worth nothing to any gate, and how a claim like 'CREATE EVENT SESSION ... ON SERVER fails with error 25737' came to carry an ellipsis exactly where the statement body belongs. A probe is that same claim with the ellipsis filled in. Every probe runs against a scratch database created for this skill and dropped after it, so a probe is free to build the fixture it needs, and no probe has to clean up after itself. Which substrate that scratch database lives on is already declared by `validation.target`, so a probe never restates it. Claims about what a MODEL says do not belong here at all: those are `value_probe.states` and `value_probe.refutes`, which already have a grader that reads exactly that shape, and mixing the two is what made this field unrunnable in the first place.

sql.description: One complete, runnable T-SQL statement or batch, executed with an administrative connection against the scratch database. No ellipsis, and no placeholder the runner cannot bind: a statement with a gap in it is the prose problem again, wearing a field name that promises otherwise. Where a claim needs a fixture, build it in the same batch rather than describing it in `setup`, and where a batch produces more than one result set, `expect` is read against the last one. Required unless `cmd` is given in its place. The keywords this repository's schema validator implements cannot express required-unless, so that half is stated here and enforced by review until a linter check lands.

cmd.description: A complete shell command line, for the claims that are about a tool rather than about the engine, such as whether bcp is present in the tools image and prints its banner with no live connection. This is the alternative to `sql`, never a companion to it.

where.description: Which machine a `cmd` probe runs on. ABSENT MEANS `container`, and that default lives in eval/lib/probe.mjs rather than in a `default` keyword here, because this repository's schema validator refuses keywords it does not implement: a `default` in the schema would read as enforced when nothing reads it, and it matters more than it looks. `container` is the default and is right for a tool the engine image ships, such as bcp: the claim is that the image carries it. `host` is right for a client tool a developer installs separately, such as SqlPackage, which is not in the image and never will be. Five probes shipped on 2026-09-02 without this field and every one failed with `sqlpackage: command not found`, because they were written by running the tool on a laptop and then executed inside a container. Ignored for `sql` probes, which always run against the engine.

expect.description: Exactly one of the four below. Two of them together is a probe whose author had not decided what it measures, and the available schema keywords cannot forbid that, so the count is a review rule until a linter check lands.

error.description: The engine error number the statement must fail with. Prefer this shape wherever it is available: a number is unambiguous where message text is a moving target across builds. A probe asserting the WRONG number is worse than no probe, because it fails loudly for a reason nobody will trust twice, so write one only where the skill's own measured evidence states the number or Microsoft Learn does.

rows.description: The result set the statement must return, one entry per row. An empty array asserts the statement returns nothing, which is a real and frequently load-bearing outcome rather than a degenerate one: a filter predicate hiding the row its own author just wrote is measured exactly this way.

succeeds.description: The statement must complete without error, and nothing is asserted about what came back. The weakest of the three. Worth using where the claim genuinely is that a statement is accepted, such as a scoped configuration the skill depends on still existing, and not worth using to pad a count.

warning.description: A severity 10 message number the statement must emit while still succeeding. Use this when the engine's answer is a warning rather than a refusal, for example Msg 1945 on an index key wider than the limit. This needs sqlcmd's -m-1: without it a severity 10 message prints its text and no number, so nothing can see it, and -b never sets a non-zero exit below severity 11. A succeeds-probe reports any warning it saw rather than failing on it, so use this shape when the warning IS the claim.

why.description: What this probe proves, and why it is worth a round trip against a live engine. A probe that cannot say why it exists is a probe nobody will maintain. When the number it asserts changes under some future engine build, this sentence is what tells the next reader whether the probe was wrong or the product moved, so name the measurement it came from where the skill has one.

engine.description: `cmd` probes only, and only where the command genuinely opens a database connection. `sql` probes run against the scratch database by construction and must NOT carry this field. It exists because `preview` requires engine evidence and nothing in a shell command's shape says whether it contacted an engine: `dab --version` and a `dab start` that serves rows out of the scratch database are both `cmd`. The claim is checked, not taken: scripts/check-maturity-drift.mjs fails a probe that declares it and whose body carries neither a credential nor the PROBE_PORT the lane hands a host probe, because a probe that opens a connection has to say who it is connecting as. That does not catch every lie and is not meant to; it catches the one that matters, which is a decorative probe relabelled to clear a gate.

triggering.description: Evals before content. At least three scenarios including one negative control, so a skill is written against measured failures rather than imagined ones.

negative.description: Prompts this skill must NOT fire on. Without these, a broad description scores well and routes badly.
